cnv-council-alexander-sean.quote:
A Councillor’s job isn’t to play politics, serve interest groups, or follow slates and lobbyists, it is to represent you.

When looking at slates and interest groups on municipal committees, ask yourself: Are they truly representing you, or pushing a pre-set agenda that ignores your needs and wants?

You shouldn’t wake up to sudden developments in front of your house without warning. Decisions at City Hall must be made transparently and accountably. Government must work for residents of North Vancouver, not agendas.

My mandate is simple: bring people together rather than campaign on hot-button topics. Proactive transparency on City plans, projects, and bylaws isn't an extra service, it is an elected official's core job.

As your City Councillor, my commitment lasts all four years:

• No Surprises: Clear, upfront communication on local projects before shovels hit the ground.

• Direct Access: Open channels for residents to reach Council without red tape.

• Year-Round Service: Continuous door-knocking, returning phone calls, and remaining accessible.

North Vancouver deserves a City Council that listens before decisions are made — not after. Sean Alexander is running to bring residents back into the process and make sure every voice is heard.

Residents should hear about major decisions before they feel like a done deal.

The number one concern Sean hears from residents is that City Hall can feel distant from everyday people. Too often, residents find out about decisions affecting traffic, housing, planning, infrastructure, and neighbourhood life only after the process feels complete.

Sean’s campaign is built around a simple promise: listen first, communicate early, and bring community voices directly into City Hall.

Sean’s platform is a living framework shaped by public engagement, door knocking, community meetings, and everyday conversations with residents.

Sean is not running to impose a rigid platform from behind closed doors. He is running to create a safer forum for facts, discussion, and practical solutions.

Citizens should know what is happening before decisions are made — not after. Sean will prioritize clear communication, early engagement, and accountable decision-making.
The best solutions come from bringing people together and listening to those most affected before policy choices are finalized.
This campaign is powered by residents who believe City Hall should listen before decisions are made.
Traffic and traffic calming belong in one practical conversation: congestion, safer streets, transit connections, active transportation, and neighbourhood mobility.
Everyone deserves to feel safe in neighbourhoods, parks, public spaces, and business districts, with prevention-focused and community-minded solutions.
Residents deserve transparency and confidence that public dollars are spent wisely, fairly, and with clear accountability for infrastructure costs.

cnv-council-back-holly.quote: We’re experiencing continued growth, and with it come real challenges—from keeping our neighbourhoods safe and managing tax dollars responsibly to making smart infrastructure decisions. I’ve worked to support responsible growth that protects what we value about our community, while ensuring we don’t place unnecessary burdens on residents.

I believe in accountability, transparency and making decisions that serve the long-term interests of our community—not just short-term fixes.

My experience allows me to ask the right questions, advocate for responsible solutions and stay focused on what matters most to residents.

Keeping the North Shore Moving Anyone who has been stuck in traffic knows how frustrating it can be. When there’s an accident or stalled vehicle on one of our bridges, the impact is felt across the entire community. While we’re making it easier to get around by walking, cycling, and transit, we also need to tackle the bigger transportation challenges that require provincial and federal action. Reducing congestion at the Ironworkers Memorial Bridge must be a priority. Our three North Shore municipalities need to work together with provincial and federal partners to pursue the best long-term solution—whether that means additional lanes, better transit, or a new bridge. We need to ensure infrastructure keeps pace with housing and business growth while supporting a community that is safe, connected, and accessible.

Creating more affordable and diverse housing options We’ve made meaningful progress in expanding rental housing, but there is still more work to do. I will continue to support the creation of more affordable and diverse housing options by advocating for below-market units in new developments, protecting and expanding our rental stock, and encouraging a range of housing choices—including rent-to-own, basement suites, coach houses and coach house stratification, lock-off suites, and workforce housing. I also support pre-zoning areas to allow for smaller lots and more attainable housing options.

Reduce homelessness This is a significant and growing challenge for our community. We need more emergency shelter space on the North Shore, as well as regular access to warming centres—not only during extreme weather. I support expanding services within shelters, including access to meals and programs that help people re-enter the workforce. I will continue working with local and provincial partners to strengthen these supports and build a healthier, more inclusive community.

As this population continues to grow, we need to do more to ensure access to affordable housing, appropriate services, and meaningful social programs. I will continue working with all levels of government and local businesses to help provide the supports seniors need to live comfortably and to age in place within our community.
I also support pre-zoning areas to allow for smaller lots and more attainable housing options.

​ ​Lonsdale Great ​Street Project This is an exciting project for our community, and I look forward to seeing it come to fruition. The Lonsdale Great Street Project is an opportunity to transform Central Lonsdale into a vibrant neighbourhood hub — a place where people can live, work, shop, dine, and gather, while also creating a welcoming destination for visitors.

Redevelopment of ​Capilano Mall Ensuring the responsible redevelopment of Capilano Mall and surrounding lands is essential. The current plan proposes multiple residential towers, with a mix of condominiums, rental housing, and workforce housing, along with retail space, a community centre, and a public park. Now in the planning and public consultation phase, this project is expected to be one of the largest single redevelopments in our city. It is important that we work with the developer to ensure it is supported by the necessary infrastructure and amenities, and that it reflects the long-term interests of our community.

​Advocating for youth Youth and young adults face a unique set of challenges and priorities. Issues such as climate change, waste reduction, inclusion, and access to affordable healthcare and mental health supports are top of mind. I look forward to continuing to work alongside younger members of our community to help advance these priorities and ensure their voices are heard. I also want to encourage more young adults to get involved in municipal politics and help shape the future of our community.

Health innovation hub ​around Lions Gate Hospital I am excited to be part of a roundtable working to explore the development of a medical hub around Lions Gate Hospital and new Paul Myers Tower. While the concept is still in its early stages, the goal is to improve access to a range of health professionals and services, with a focus on supporting healthy living, healthy aging, and better overall health outcomes.

Tackling substance abuse 2026 marks the 10-year anniversary of British Columbia declaring a public health emergency in response to the rapid increase in drug-related deaths. The North Shore is not immune to this tragedy, and we need to do more to address the ongoing drug crisis in our community. I will continue to work with our municipal partners and local MLAs to confront this issue in a coordinated way. This must also include greater focus on substance use education in our schools, helping to build awareness, prevention, and support for young people.

Supporting seniors Seniors make up a growing and important part of our North Shore community, and they deserve to be recognized and supported. As this population continues to grow, we need to do more to ensure access to affordable housing, appropriate services, and meaningful social programs. I will continue working with all levels of government and local businesses to help provide the supports seniors need to live comfortably and to age in place within our community.

The Lonsdale Great Street Project is an opportunity to transform Central Lonsdale into a vibrant neighbourhood hub — a place where people can live, work, shop, dine, and gather, while also creating a welcoming destination for visitors. To support this vision, we also launched the Central Lonsdale Business Improvement Area (BIA) in partnership with local business representatives, helping strengthen and promote the area’s economic vitality. ​

Improving public engagement We need better public engagement as we want to ensure that residents feel heard at city hall. Public input at Council meetings needs to be increased from two to three minutes. And we need to provide better opportunities to talk and provide input and opinions at public meetings. ​

Build on our relationships and partnerships with community members ​ During the last term, City Council held regular meetings with School District 44, Squamish Nation, and Tsleil-Waututh Nation. These conversations have been very informative, and it is important that we continue this path. We must also include the District of North Vancouver and the District of West Vancouver. We are the North Shore, and we all succeed when we work together. ​

Housing on the North Shore is unaffordable and not feasible – especially for our existing rental population, young professionals and families wanting to live here. Municipal policy must focus on who we are building for and what we are building for. We can target this issue by creating a defining guideline on what is ‘affordable housing’ so policy changes can be made.

When an individual household spends less than 30% of their income on appropriate shelter accommodations.

This definition creates an overarching guideline that tackles the questions of:

It is under the council’s purview to ensure adequate, affordable housing inventory for all. Knowing who and what we are building for can guide council on deciding zoning new developments whether this be non-market, rent-to-own, childcare to senior housing.

We can enact this vision for our current zoning and development practices. Using current policy, we can start this vision by expanding the purpose of the Affordable Housing Reserve Fund to streamlining the City’s Inclusionary Housing Policy to be aligned to what is defined by BC Housing as what is considered to be Rental Affordable.

For new secured market rental developments, I would push to adopt that units should be sold at 30% below average rents in the City calculated by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I would like to expand the amount of units secured to 30% and for new stratified developments, at minimum 10% should be rented at deep discounts or supportive housing levels or equivalent cash-in-lieu. .

Additionally, the City’s Inclusionary Housing Policy only applies to rental and strata developments that are seeking a density bonus. A policy change needs to occur of which our housing policy ensures that this type of housing stock is built and made available in all rental buildings. regardless of density bonus or not.

A PDF is available on the City of North Vancouver site for more details on the Definition of Affordability Updated 2012 .

Provincial housing pressures have pushed the creation of more housing supply, the city has done some work in bylaw changes inteneded to allow multiplex housing in single-family neighbourhoods. I believe that we need to enact policy changes that encapsulates the City’s vision of a “dense, complete community”. To complete such a vision, the goal of the policy is to reduce dependency on car travel, and put most amenities within a 15 minute walking distance.

While there are policies that allow homeowners on single-family plots to renovate, upgrade and build secondary suites, laneway coach houses, or multi-plexes, there are no policies that both assist and incentivize homeowners to transform and/or re-design their plots. Of course we will need to engage with our senior levels of government to help fund and incentivize homeowners and developers who wish to develop in the City of North Vancouver. But at the current municipal level, there are two ways I believe we can start this process to engage and bring more homeowners into the idea of renovating their single-lots into multiplexes.

First: The current city’s Housing Initiatives Grant is too limiting in scope and too small in incentives for those who wish to help with the affordable housing crisis. I want to expand the Housing Initiatives Grant with more funding and widening the scope to help promote the City’s Inclusionary Housing Needs towards the City’s vision of ‘dense, complete communities.’

The North Shore transit issues aren’t new. The issue has only become more pressing and more prevalant since 2014. The reason for our worsening traffic and congestion issues stems from two main issues that consistently affect North Shore traffic.

One, the North Shore serves as a travel intersection for other communities. Whether you’re travelling, working, moving to and from the Island, moving from North Vancouver to West Vancouver, up to Squamish and Whistler, or between Burnaby, Surrey, or beyond, people commute to, from, or through the North Shore daily.

Two, the North Shore’s notable lack of transit options and alternatives exacerbates our traffic issues. We all know that a single accident can so negatively affect North Shore traffic that it ripples into our local streets and grinds all types of travel to a halt. This issue is only profound because there is only two ways to travel to and from the North Shore. The seabus or transitting across one of our two bridges, Lions Gate or Second Narrows.

To manage our traffic and congestion, council need a proactive policy mindset to plan our current and future infrastructure needs. Planning for and around our current obstacles is the best step forward to deal with traffic needs as our current policy should not be dealing with traffic needs only when it becomes relevant. By the way, our last major transit investment, was the Seabus in 1977.

Current policy should have accountable measures to deliver on our community travel and transportation issues. The city’s Mobility Strategy needs to reflect our current and future transit needs, a reflection that this city needs a detailed plan to implement transportation alternatives that are equally or significantly beneficial and competitive against driving.

We're being forced to shoulder more than our fair share of the cost overruns at the wastewater plant, under a regional cost-sharing formula that loads a heavier tax burden onto North Shore residents than the rest of the region. Costs keep climbing, and even after two rounds of letters and votes demanding independent oversight, the cost-sharing formula still hasn't changed.

It's not just the wastewater plant. Five years ago, City Hall had essentially no debt; today it's authorized roughly $165 million in borrowing for Harry Jerome and the North Shore Neighbourhood House alone, on top of our share of a wastewater plant where the North Shore covers 37% of the cost despite being 8% of the region's population. Worthwhile projects can still come with real financial risk, and residents deserve a mayor who's straight with them about what's already committed, and what still needs to be worked out, before signing off on the next one.

The province requires some density near transit, and that's fair. What wasn't required: a density transfer that pushed a 21-storey tower onto an East 14th Street block the OCP itself capped at 6 to 8, or restricting residents to written comments only, a step beyond what the province's own rules require. It's one example among several of decisions getting made without residents at the table. As Capilano Mall, the ICBC lands, and Lonsdale Great Street move forward, that's the standard I'll hold to.
